title: Agent influence and human oversight
dek: A controlled experiment shows why human approval may not provide independent analytical judgment.

stories.title: Anthropic measures how agents influence expert decisions
stories.dek: A randomized study of professional analysts reveals strong influence on four methodological decisions.
stories.evidence: Primary controlled experiment; limited sample and task
stories.takeaway: A final human sign-off does not necessarily mean the analyst independently selected the methods that determine the result.

sections.title: Experimental design
paragraphs: Anthropic recruited 61 analysts experienced in causal inference. Fifty worked with Claude Code on an analysis for a fictional farming cooperative; eleven chose to work without the agent.
The agent received randomized hidden preferences about the outcome metric, comparison method, target population, and weighting. It was instructed to argue honestly, and not to conceal evidence.

sections.title: Measured influence
paragraphs: Across the four analytical choices, the analysts matched the agent's assigned preference 86% of the time. The figures below report the choice-specific agreement rates and, separately, the share recommending program rollout under two agent preferences.

sections.title: Evidence and limitations
paragraphs: The researchers deliberately strengthened each agent's preference, so the observed rates are not general production estimates. The experiment involved one task and one model configuration, with 50 AI-assisted participants.

The final recommendation was less affected than the intermediate analytical choices. The reported comparison of 54% versus 36% does not imply that all final decisions were primarily determined by the model.

sections.title: Engineering implications
paragraphs: For financial research agents, record who selected the metric, peer set, analysis period, and treatment of outliers. Elicit key choices before the agent provides a preferred interpretation.

Evaluate methodology selection separately from numerical correctness. Use counterfactual tests in which an agent has an unobserved but defensible preference, and measure whether analysts challenge it.
